blocks.x: Bill Matthews, you can start anytime you wish and tell us a little bit about your life, when you were born, where and so on.

Bill Matthews, as old man Bill Matthews speaking, one of the New Orleans original who has been playing jazz for over 40 years, is still going strong, 1959. Born of New Orleans original drummers, 1915 to 1919, it was Alphonse P. Q. Suggestions, you were a young man Billy, my boy, why don't you learn some other instrument. So I've taken P. Q. advice, my choice was trombone. But before I quit playing drums, I was playing with some of the New Orleans best jazz bands. 1915, Buddy Petit, one of New Orleans jazz trumpet players. King Dooson, trombonist, former of Buddy Bowling. Kid René, one of Louis Armstrong's jazz boys that come up together. Jack Carey, known as King of the World as Tiger Ray. And old man Joe Johnson, one of the best trumpet players we ever had in the city of New Orleans. So sweet and so mellow. And old Sammy Morgan come along. Sammy had the best go here. Sammy did wonderful with his orchestra. Well, old man Robichaud picked me up, John Robichaud. I joined John Robichaud as drummer. I played with him a while.
Did you work at the Lyric Theater with him or in the dance band? Did you work in the theater with him or with Robichaud?
No, out of West End.
West End.

West End. West End. And so Frankie Dooson come over to hear the band. He was working at the West End Country Club. Frankie Dooson come over to hear the band. And he said, Billy, you come on with me. I want you to come to the roadhouse. Jim Toms Roadhouse. That's really a fact. So I went over to Jim Toms Roadhouse. We didn't have no union then at that time. You do what you want. Quit the night. So I went over to Jim Toms Roadhouse and I played with Frankie Dooson Orchestra. Mutt Carey was on cornet. Old Mutt Carey. I knew Mutt. Henry Mutt was on drums. I just remember. Buddy Christian was on piano and banjo.
Yeah, I knew him in New York too. Nice guy.

And we stuck around there, old Frankie Dooson. Stayed there a little while. So here comes Walter Deku. Next block from the woman to play at the bungalow. So I go ahead and work. I jump in for a little more money. Them times, you know, money was money. Dollar was a dollar. Sure. So the Walter Deku line up was. Old Man Dutre on clarinet. Old Man Joe Howard on cornet. Walter Deku on piano and myself on drums. And Big Eye Louie on clarinet. Old Man Dutre is a double. Big Eye Louie couldn't double. Well, that went on through that way. And AJ and Peter are going to come along. And say, Billy. They all call me Billy. I want you to work over at the Trashina. But say, I'll give you $15 a week. $15 was big money them days. Yeah. And you knock off oil. You go to work at 8. Knock off at 12. All over time, you get paid for it. So Piron had a pretty good line up. I was a young fella. And then jumping from place to place. There's nowhere to go. Looking for the money. So I went over there with Piron. And Steve Lewis. I met Steve Lewis on my way coming in town in West End Court. I said, Steve, I'm going to play with Piron. He said, well, I'm going to play with Piron myself. When you're going to start that? I said, tomorrow night. He said, I'm going to start that too tomorrow night. I said, at that time, Piron had a, had T.O. on clarinet. And Peter Bocards on trombone and violin. Piron on violin. And Walter, that fella lived in Kansas City. He was playing piano. And Louie Warner on saxophone. He had Udall on piano. That's a Udall. He was playing piano. So when he made a switch, an old man can't travel. He said, well, old man can't travel is going to New York. He's going to take a trip to New York. That's the getaway. So he didn't see them going to New York. He went to play at the Larry's Theater with old man Robichaud. That's why. He didn't go to New York. So I stayed out there until we got tired. Procbition come through there and bootlegging and chaseless all around, different places. So the West End Tavern opened up a new place. Papa Celestine, Half Ones Piku, Steve Lewis and myself and Hemp Benson. Hemp Benson was the manager. Old trombone player. So Hemp, choice us and we went on to play at the West End Tavern with them. Papa wasn't doing anything then. He didn't have no band of his own. So we stuck around there at the West End Tavern until Uncle Sam opened up the joint out there with the soldiers, the sailors, closed down everything. So that lasts about six to eight months like that. Here come another break come through. Jack Sheen, he opened up and he said, Rizzley, get me a band. I ain't been a bit of Rizzley. I want a bunch of young men. I went on, he choice me and I went with Rizzley. Played drum with Rizzley a while until the wolf come out there and closed down the gambling and bootlegging. Place they call it out there and highway there. Jack Sheen's, it's called Jack Sheen's Place.
Is that from the Beverly?

Beverly Garden. That's Beverly Garden. So we had mean old man, Kimball and all of us. Papa Celestine, he went with Rizzley too. And we left Hampton Benson, I originally being a trauma player at South. And T.O., he quit P-Rone, he went on over there with us too. So we stuck out there and- You played drums then? He stuck out there a long time, making good money. So well, the boys got to say they want to go back to the red light. Went on back to the red light and played at King Holler. King Holler was at Pete Lawler's playing there with Mac and Mac and their Mac Mac show. At King Holler, Buddy Krishna on piano, Omer Valtu on violin. The band in them days didn't have a violin. Didn't have no leader. A lot of them was leaning. Henry Zeno on drum. I remember that. No bass. While the floor show was going pretty good. And one night, we goes through there and Henry Zeno laid off. He didn't lay off the standing time. I said, come on, rest me up man. So he went to gambling. He never did come back. So that's when Joe started to organ with Mary. Mary Mac and Mac. He said, that's my homeboy. We all from our years. We all was sticking together, playing together. We got along. So Henry come on back. So they fired Henry for me. At least I knew Henry was a first class drummer, but I was a younger man than Henry. That's all. So Mac said, well we going to make a trip. Will you come with us? I said, I don't mind. I said, but I'm learning how to play trombone now. I'm going to play trombone. She said, sure. I said, what's the idea? I said, well old man Piku and I was going out to West End there one night. He said, man, you a young man. Why don't you learn how to play something before you get to a low, them drums all around. I said, I take no peak. We used to call him peak. Pike. I take Pike's advice. I pick up the trombone. I started to pull around with the trombone. I said, well I'm going to Vic Gasper. So Vic was one of the greatest baritone players and trombone players in the city of New Orleans. I said, will you teach me a pop? He said, sure. Come on. Come on. Asked Creole. I went to Vic's house. He bought me a catechism. Not a catechism. Imperial record. Method. With no horn. So he took me over to Method and I called All I Know So Good. I didn't know much of bass clip music but I knew plenty of treble clipped because I used to play bells with my drums. Oh, yeah, sure. So I went over to bass clip music and two weeks after he told me, get your horn pops. That's all you need is a horn. That's all right. That's all. I went over there and I said my friend Harrison Barnes. I said, Harry, I'm going to learn how to play trombone. I learned how to your horn. He said, I got a whole horn, yeah. I said, it'll slide in much. So you can have the bells. I come on up to town, you're ready to play old Jack Carey at his barbershop. I said, Jack, you got an old trombone on the line, play trombone. He said, yeah, take both or take yours. There's one, take one. So Jack's slide was good but I used the Harrison Barnes bell and Jack's slide, put it together. I went to Vic Gasper house. I run through the method so quick. In two weeks time, Vic told me, leave the book home, pops. Well, I left the book home and he had some of his orchestration music with John Robeshow and him using the brass in the orchestra. Went over to music. He said, oh, pops, you don't need the more less. You know more music than what I do. He said, I wish I ever learned as much as you do. So finally, I start to fool around with the horn. I was going so fast with it by playing in the orchestra, drumming the orchestra. I know all them numbers that was playing, like all them old numbers. I know them. The tempo of them, I couldn't go wrong. It wasn't like a fella just had to pick up the instrument. So, I went on. So, one day they were short in the brass band. My brass band, my exhaustive brass band. So, Vic Gasper said, pop, you bring that old trombone and bring your brother on drum. I said, what one do you want? What one of my brothers? He said, well, any one you want, bring them. So, I used my older brother, Remus Manchin, because he was a good street drummer, first-class street drummer. So, I told him, I said, come on, bud. I used to call him buddy, come on, bud, make this money. I'm going to play trombone today. My first job out. I said, who told you that? I said, oh, man, Vic Gasper. He's going to be right there even to play in the barrow, huh? So, I knew all the marches and things, how they go. I knew all the marches and things, how they go and everything. I couldn't go wrong. I went on through so good. So, Harrison Barnes said, you know, I work in the D. We was living right across the street from each other and said, I work in the D. I mean, I can't get off. you gonna be the trombone player in the brass band. I said, okay, Harry, and use your brother on snare drums. I said, all right. We did that so often and so often. One day, we was playing the parade down on La Perue Street on a Sunday evening. I was playing the trombone at an armature on trumpet. And had old man, George Moret, on trumpet. And they said, we got to get another trumpet player. I said, why don't you try to dip him out? He said, man, he can't read. He said, well, he'll make out just like he'll make out. So I took my advice and said, we can't go out with no two trumpets because it's going to be all day parade. So I went on by Louis back there. Back then, I found Louis. I said, Louis, you gonna play in the brass band tomorrow? He said, oh, man, you know I can't make that. I can't make no brass band. I have a Dick Salsa band. You know that stuff. I said, we can play no music tomorrow. He ain't going to play. It's the only way you can get in through there and learn how to play that music. I said, all right. You there. I said, sure, I'm going to play trombone. I said, that's all right. I can play as much music in this corner as you can on the trombone. I know I can. That's Louis' turn. So got back down La Perru Street, back there by Muley's. Muley's wasn't running there, but another fellow was running there. That big jumbo bottle was a nickel. Louis took a big jumbo bottle and drank it down. He never did drink. And drank it down. Then he had the cramps. Had to lay Louis out. Louis got overheated and had the cramps for that jumbo bottle. He stayed right there. So we went and piddled on through with our, with our Louis. We went on through. So I made so good. At night I was coming to work right around the corner of you at the Muley and Willow. I was coming in to play with old man Humphrey. Willie Humphrey's daddy. Old man Humphrey. Is that Jim Humphrey?
Mm-hmm.
old man, a clarinet player.
Oh really?

He still let it play with him that night and we had a double band. So me and John Joseph was on the bass and everything, so he said, Bill can you get another clarinet big band's coming back. I said sure, I can get red. They said come on Biffley, we call him Biffley. I said come on baby, we got a job tonight man. He said well, we're going to play against Kid Ora and them. Kid Ora and Oliver back at Me and Willa. Who was the trumpet?
Red.

Red Allen. Red Allen. We call him Biffley. I said he come on back there man, we blowed him out. We blowed him out, so these only had one trumpet, Ora had one trumpet, that was with Joe, that's all. I said Joe called us all kind of little young names as he always did, all kind of little young names and that's a human order had it. He had a few words about it. He wanted some more help. Ora said the jobs don't pay enough to have all that kind of help. I'm going to get mine. So he said yeah, let's get this little boy Lewis, get Lewis Armstrong to play with us. We going to kill New Orleans and kill him dead. Joe don't speak to me but Joe talk bad. He said we going to kill him dead. So finally they used, Joe, Joe used, Louis Armstrong on some engagements and there was the two best jazz trumpet players in the city of New Orleans. Louis Armstrong and Joe Oliver. Louis can tell you all about that. He know where he started from. So finally things went on good so Joe and Mac, Mary Mac had a few words down there and Joe said he was leaving. Joe left. Joe said when I come back to New Orleans, Jared Thomas would be the mayor. Jared Thomas would be president of the booze club. When I come back to New Orleans, Jared Thomas would be mayor. So when I finally again I saw Joe, he was down in Quincy, Florida. He had never come back no more. Never been made back. He had no further than Biloxian went back. He had Paul Barnes playing with him. Paul Barnes, Paul Barbaran. He had a bunch of New Orleans brothers come right to Biloxian and didn't come back to New Orleans. So when I finally heard that Joe was dead and we went on through. So one day I was playing my parade. Amos White, he come along, another great trumpet player. Amos White said, Billy, how about make the trip with me? I said, well, I was single and I didn't care where they go. He said, do North Louisiana man. Let's get away from you. Things just get tight. So we made up a band to go with old man Andrew Foster. He used to be a road band. That's where we went. My brother, baby, he was well. He said, well, Billy, I said, what? I said, you're going up there about Joe and him now. I know I ain't going to see you no more. Lewis and all of them up there. I said, I said, I don't say that man. It's like that. On a Sunday evening. So I went on, took my suitcase and I went. I was in Kansas City, Missouri on that Christmas Eve night. I got a telegram number. My brother was dead, buried today. So I didn't see him anymore. Which brother? Is that? That brother, baby. So I didn't see him anymore. So I kept going. I said, well, no need to come back. I kept going. I can't see him anymore. So I got around Kansas City, Missouri, played around there a little while. So this old boy plays so much banjo. He's young. With Nattoes. All of us, they're all young, all young. So I went through Oklahoma. He stayed in Oklahoma about 15 months. Bowling, Oklahoma. First time I ever saw a woman be mayor of a little time. So finally we went there and stayed there. It was doing so good. And we got a wire from Charlie Crest to come on to St. Louis, Billy. I've been knowing Charlie a long time. He's on the boat. He said, come on to St. Louis, Bill. So I went over to St. Louis. Then he put me in the jazz land, playing with him. So that's why our little band broke up. Amos White went to California. He's still in Oakland, California. Yes, I saw him. So he gave up with me.
Fess and I got two visits with him.
We were all left together. Frank Pass and all of us left. Nobody come back home but me. So while I come back home-
Who was leader of that band? Was that Nat Toe?
Nat Toe. He was the leader.
Nat Toe.

Nat Toe was the bass player. Nat Toe stuff evening. I went on to Cincinnati Journal, I like to come back to New Orleans. And I come back and I settle down there. And it was going so good. I played with Sidney a little while, but Sidney was a funny fellow with that stuff, you know. Yeah, I've heard that. That money. Yeah, I've heard that. The old Roche, we call him Roche. Roche liked that money so well. He messed with the money so much. So me and little McCollum, George McCollum, nice little trumpet player, made up a good bunch of fellas and started playing around here. And the next thing we did so well, so Papa Celestine grabbed me. And Papa grabbed me there. I stayed right there with Papa. Papa said, you want money? I said, sure money. You want work? I said, sure. So I stayed right there with Papa Celestine. He had Ernest Kelly playing trauma with him. And Papa was improving himself then. The guy, Kelly, and myself, and him, made good. So I stayed right there with Papa until things got good and bad, good and bad. Who else was in the, who was the piano at that time? The piano at time? Jeanette? Jeanette Salve. She was a piano at that time. Emma Barris was a piano of Risley's Tuxedo. I see. See, Papa didn't have a band too long. See? Who played clarinet or sax with you?
With Risley? Well, with both of the bands, you might tell. Oh yeah. So Pete, uh, Teo, Lorenzo Teo was playing

out of Jack Sheen, like I told you. Yeah. With Risley. See? And then they left there. See? And Teo still stuck with Risley until things got good. Then he went, jumped over to Pete Ron again. Then he went to New York. And that's where he went to New York and he never did come back. Stay there. He died there. His wife there, Pete's sister, she played bass too. So that's why. So that's where that happened with Papa Celestan in Risley. Well, did Teo's wife play bass? Sure. I never knew that. That's Peter Burkard's sister. I knew that. But Peter never told us that. We talked to Peter. Oh, Pete never did tell you that? He never told us that, no. But the wonderful bass player. Really? In the bands? She played with the bands. Oh, man. She's a wonderful bass player. Oh, Pete knows that. And so as we went on, let's see, where was I at? That's about who the saxes were with Celestan. Yeah, about Papa Celestan. So it's Papa Celestan grabbing. So that's where I settled down. And then we goes on, straightened our band. We got on a boat, a little boat they call, a pleasure boat they call New Orleans, the Greater New Orleans. And it worked them and did so well. And they closed that boat down. So we used to go over to Biloxi every year for five three years of White House from the Universal Hotel. And so I got married. Did you have any sax
players in that band, Bill? Who was that? Did you have any saxophone players? Saxophone players? Saxophone, sure.

Who was playing on the sax? Well, I remember the first on the saxophone had Joe Rouget, Edmund Hall. Edmund Hall. Oh, yeah. And Clarence Hall. See? So Edmund Hall, he jumped down and they took Earl Peterson. He don't play anymore. He's on the road now. He's a- We met him on a train, yeah. Yeah. And then after that, well, that's the way it's switched up about. But our first band was with Papa Celestine. And we did that recording and all of that. My Josephine and all of that. That was Paul Bones. My Josephine and all of that. My Josephine and all of that. My Josephine and all of that. This boy is sing. I just remember his name. Aida Cheri. No, not Aida Cheri. That's Sidney- Correa or something? That's Sidney Correa, Simon Moreira, John Moreira, August Russo, I think. I was known as Josephine. August Russo, I think it was playing as Josephine. Who was the second trumpet?
Who played?
Second trumpet at that time. Let me see. With Papa Celestine was the second trumpet. I know it wasn't Guy because Guy wasn't, Guy hadn't come to New Orleans yet. How was Sniety? Sniety. Sniety.
Have a Sniety. Did you ever make any records with Kid Schatz or Ricard Alexis? Ricard Alexis? Was he on any of those?
Oh, that was Papa Celestine. We recorded for A La Bar and Maryland and High Society. The real old ones. I mean the real old band though in the 1920s.
Was Ricard on?
That's who Ricard was the one playing second trumpet with Papa Celestine and made that Josephine. That's what it was. Ricard, he was playing. Ricard made that Ricard. That's fine. That's good.
Did the Shots Madison ever play on the records with you in the old days? Ricard. Shots. You know, Shots. Kid Schatz Madison. All you talking about Shots? Shots. Oh, sure. Was he on the records?

Not with me. Not on the records. Shots never didn't leave Ricard. Shots was stuck with Ricard. He stayed with Ricard. Shots and this boy, uh, but this boy, uh, played trombone. Well, they all stuck with Ricard. Yeah. David Jones and them, they stayed on the Pelican with Ricard. Emma Barris, all them John Porter, they all stayed with Ricard on the Pelican. Yeah. Papa Celestine and David Ricard fell out for one dollar. Really? That's right. That's why they made the split. They won one large dollar. That's why they made the split. So Papa made his band. That's why they made two Tuxedo bands. Celestine Tuxedo bands and Rizzley Tuxedo bands. So finally, Rizzley's already existing now, but still living. Yeah. Papa, he's gone forever. So we did fine with Papa's new big band. And we went on through and I just settled down. Here and then, got married and stuck around and the pressure comes through. In and out, in and out, you understand? Working in and out, gig work, play every place around. I knew all these you could play. And the boy started splitting up. Guy went away and Paul Bones went away, you know. So I just split up like that. So I just made a great change. So, and things was really dead, dead, dead, me and Happy. We stuck with Celestine. All the big time, they had them quit. So Papa said, I'm going to make a comeback. I said, what you going to do now? I was waiting at the shipyard then. So I said, he's going to make a comeback. So yeah, let's get through together and make a rehearsal. I said, now what you going to do now, man? So my wife said, oh man, you are, told him over the telephone. Oh man, you ought to go sit down and rush your noise. My same little wife in the back there. So he just laughed over the telephone. So we made a couple of rehearsals. We got Ricard on bass, Piku on clarinet, and myself on trumpet, and Pop on trumpet, Black Happy on drums, and Moistad D Fields on piano. That was the comeback band. Yeah, we rehearsed that pop. I rehearsed it twice, three times a week. So finally, Pop made a comeback, and Johnny Corrin started the book and Papa Celestine. And we got together and started coming back, coming back, coming back, grassland. So there Pop, Celestine, Ricard got a job at the paddock, where his little brother was working. His little brother Lester played drums. He had a combo there. He had a job at the paddock and said, Mr. Villaner wanted to try a Dixley band. Who could I get in touch with? So he brought Ricard to see him, Mr. Villaner. And Ricard called me up 12 o'clock that night. So he got a job, man, on Bourbon Street. That was in 49. That was around May the 10th. May the 8th or 9th. So we're going to start Saturday night. So that was on May the 10th. So I was taking Papa Celestine, myself, and Happy. And we had to get a good Dixland piano player. And he didn't want no women to play piano. So Ricard said, I'm going to get Octave Crosby. So Celestine said, you get who you want. I'm not going to leave my band out here. I'm not going to play there to help you to build it up. That's what he said, because I got too much work coming up. He said, Billy, you going to be with me? You and Happy. I said, yeah, we're going to come. We ain't going to leave. It's like that. So things went on the first six months at the paddock. Celestine worked on the Ricard. So, let's start working on the Ricard.

And the next six months Celestine had taken the job over from Ricard. And that threw at Ricard and made everything go to Papa Celestine. You see? Everything was Papa Celestine. So Papa Celestine was sick then. I know he was very sick then. So he worked there a few years and got himself straightened out. And he stopped to fool him around. He didn't want to work anymore, you know. Didn't know how to quit. So finally he jumped down. So Houston, he burst a little to the board. Houston said, what do you want to do? He said, I want to make, I want to get my band in here. So he had another band on our side. Certain men he wanted to get in there to work.
That's Fats, Fats Houston? No, Celestine. Celestine.

Yeah, Papa. So he said, I want to get some other fellas to work with. So he thought he was all tired of it, Mr. Steve Leonard. Mr. Steve Leonard would do anything he said he would do. So Houston said, what do you want a week? So Papa Celestine said, I want $300 a week. That time he was getting $70. He said, I want $300 a week for myself. So I told him, I said, well, Papa, you know, you don't want to work there. He said, well, you're right, Billy. You're right. I don't want to work there. He said, if you give me $300 a week, I'll work. And I'll work with my other band. He said, what do you intend to do? I said, I'm going to stick on the job where I'm working at. I'm working with Ricard. Ricard Broaddus here. And I'm working and making a great improvement in it.
See?

He said, you get on out there and make another band of yourself. That's all you can do. Be okay with me. Anytime I happen to need you, I'll ask you for a job. That's all I can do. Until now. Pop me up in a little band until now. I'm still at the paddock.
Yeah. All right. So much out.
See you. You know that.
Before I come home. You didn't tell about Jelly. That was around St. Louis, was it?

Well, that's around St. Louis. Only one I know in the band, the Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll was on the road there. He had an old bus. And I was living out on Phoenix with old man Kimball. Old man Kimball, the bass player. So he said, well, Billy, I'm going to join Jelly. I ain't doing nothing. I'm going to join Jelly Roll. And from there, make a trip with him. I said, well, Pop, when you're going back home? He said, well, anywhere is my home now. My son is raised now. That's a little bit of Kimball, a banjo player. He said, my son is raised now. I don't care. Anywhere is my home. So he joined Jelly Roll, him and Dawes, several other fellas I know. Harry Dolls and all that. They joined Jelly Roll. Jelly Roll come from Chicago over there to pick up a bunch. So I said, well, I'm not going right now. I said, I'm going to stick you up in Charlotte Crescent and make this money. I said, Papa Foster said, look, don't you go before you stay here. You stay right here. Stay right here. So finally they made a tour about, say about four months or so. They come right back to St. Louis. And they come out to St. Louis. They was down. That's why the boys jumped down from Jelly Roll. So I got kind of funny myself about St. Louis. So Jelly said, Billy, I said, what do you say, Fred? His name is Fred Mouton. I'll call him Jelly. I said, well, anytime you come to Chicago, you look me up. Here's my address. I said, sure, I'll do that. He said, I'm going. He said, so Jelly was kind of a smart guy. He was all pigeon-toed stuff. He was pigeon-toed. Kind of smart old red guy. So I brought him up. He's come out of the house and talked to me. He said, what do I want you to do for me? Before he asked me for any money for transportation, he put that question to me about coming to Chicago. I said, I want you to give me an advance me back to Chicago. I said, you should ask me that in front. Go and come jive me like that, you know. I said, you know, we're all home for it. He said, you be back down by Ironton after a while. I said, it's home, Ironton. Ironton, Louisiana right down. His home was not in Northern. What town? Ironton. About 12 miles from here. Down the road. Down the river farther or which way? That little road used to go down. They don't run down. Round, round, finest down that way. Little town they call it Ironton. That's Jolly Road home.
That's what I didn't know.
Jolly Road and Jimbo. Jimbo. That's the damn one of the cutouts. Jimco and all that. All that.
Down that way.

Down toward Buras. Down that way. That's down that way. Yeah. So I told him, I said, well, yeah, sure. I'll give you a fare. Went to the station. Went to the station. He got his ticket and everything. And I gave him two extra dollars. Because I was planning on going to Chicago anyway. You know? Yeah. So I said, well, before I could go to Chicago, I'm going to, you know, straighten things out where I want to live at. In Chicago. So that's the break I had. So I went to Chicago. Over to Jolly. I mean, I went on to give Jolly his money. And Jolly got home. He wrote me back a nice letter and everything. And two weeks after that, Jolly sent me $10 bill. Yeah. And any time I'm coming to Chicago, I'd be welcome to his house. Jolly was welcome. He said, well, find home and everything. But at that time, he was down. I was pushing travel on the road. That's Johnny's instrument. And Herbert Lindsey on violin. Well, they both died. Now Herbert, both of them died in Chicago. Yeah. And he went and he kept on going big then. And him and when I played again, I was big enough to go around then, you see. So he made me help him through third district fair to bring his drums. I went with him several times, but that first time he went to third district fair to go by the economy hall. And he climbed to my hall and I stayed there all night, see. And they made me play something there with Old Man, Marion Parade's name, see. That's the break me and Buddy Johnson, all of us was from Algeist. And Jimmy Pala, see he was from Algeist too, he was leading the band there. He was from Algeist. That was before Pete was leading. Pete used to lead the superior band too. But Jimmy was before Pete, see. And Jimmy used to play alto, toot-toot horn in the brass band and violin in the orchestra. All musicians was doubling up on the streets and this. They didn't like now, they just take one or two numbers and say they know everything. It wasn't like that in the damn days. He was trying to learn something.
Where did you live in Algiers? What street?

Born and raised all of us. Born on 719 Newton Street. Every child my mother had, born and raised right there. On Newton Street. All of them born right there. None born in the Chaddawson, all of us had grannies. What you call them grannies, you know. All of them. When did you move over here? Well, my first wife and I, we separated, lived together six years. And that was after I come back from off my toe and I joined Pop. Yeah. And I come back and I settled down. And the same little, the same old drummer I got now. I went to hire him. What year? Let's see, we got married, 22, 22 or 23 anyway. I went to hire him to, Pop had so much work at that time. And he said, Bill I want you to help me out to get a band to go to the Padre Royal. That was on the Mardi Gras day. Yeah. And then I said, well I know a fella. I get George. George Williams, just call him Big Hawk now. I said, I get George Williams in here. Beaks you up a good band like that. Cause Pop took us from George or from that other boy there, you know. We used to play with him, Pop took us, took me from him. So I know George was pretty good. So I said, George will get you a bunch, two or three or four of them that go to Padre Royal. That was 37. Okay. You.

So I come up town on 4th Street, I know where George was living. I said, George, you playing Mardi Gras? He said, no, no, what happened? I said, well, you can get three pieces to go to Padre Arroyo for pop. He said, yeah, yeah, let me get three pieces. I'll get three pieces. So before I saw George, this little girl here that I got from my wife, now she was sweeping off the porch. I said, lady, can you tell me where George lives? She said, yes, right down there. I'll go get it for you. And that's where I met her, right there from there. And that's my wife. Now, that's how I met her. I hope she don't regret it. No, I bet she doesn't. That's the same old George where you're playing with me now. He always tell you, I'll give you a good husband, girl. You know that. I hope you've known each other so long, me and George, you see. So after Happy, he was like Happy, we was raised together. You know each other so long when Happy was peddling coal around here, you know. He used to buy coal for me. Happy used to have a route on the river. Buy coal for me, you know, coal and some, with the time like that. Happy, been known in the family all our life, Black Happy. So we was good friends like George, the same over there, you know. So Happy got sick and so my first mind was on to give George a, think if I have anything to do. Now he's still there and doing good, see.
What was the very last job you played on drums? When the last days?

Now, well I can't, I can't exactly mention. Here in New Orleans, the last job I played on drums here in New Orleans, it was out at Trance Senior's Restaurant. Rainbag. I told P. Ron, I said, P. Ron, I'm going away. I'm going to take me a trip. I got a chance to develop all my trombone better. And Peter Bocard was out there with him and all. Playing, playing, he was playing trombone too out there. And Peter said, well that's the way, you're doing good around here. And we all used to go home together every night. I mean, Pete was like that. Sometimes we'd meet Fest, Banana. Sometimes, Charlotte Love and all of them, we'd meet them all, going home sometimes. But meet Pete was regular like that. Every night. The old West End car. So I was telling him, so he must wipe on me to go, when I'm, while I'm single like that, I'm going to make a trip, you see. You see what it's all about. And I can develop on my home. So that's the last I remember playing trap drum here in New Orleans. I was playing there in town. And again, I played. I was in Kansas City, Missouri. With Nat Tolls in there. And Frank Paschley got a rift to go out on the outskirt of town in Kansas City, Missouri. And he said, the fellow wanted drummer. Because his drummer done taken sick. Something happened, something, something in the family's deed or something like that. He said, I know you can play a drum. You just got off the drums. So, him as white said, he don't want no cornet player. So, he said, well, no, he don't want no cornet player. So, at the meantime, Frank Paschley had then hired Herbert Moran. Herbert Moran was on a trip with us too. What did Frank Paschley play? Banjo. That's the boy that's who played with the Honey Drippers. That's what I thought.

He's a tall fella in California. He played with the boy. He played with the boy. He played with the one day at the Bunk once. I heard him with Mason Records. He played with the Honey Drippers. Those records we played with Wade Whaley, Frank Paschley's own job.

So, Frank had then hired Herbert Moran because he liked Herbert Moran playing better than White because Herbert was more jazzy. We had two Trump and she had a big band traveling. So, Frank said, now, we can't hire Tom. I don't want no Thomas Taylor. Thomas Taylor's a little drummer. He's living in Chicago now. He's a drummer with us. So, you come up and play a little drum. That boy would be sick two, three nights. Make that money. So, I remember that. I went out there and the nightclub and I played. They wanted me to stay around there. So, I said, no, I was waiting for a call from St. Louis from Charlotte Crest. And I worked there three nights. I remember that. Three nights. And I took that money and I told my boys, I'm going on over there with Charlotte Crest.
That's for that.
I lived 27-27, Garfield. That's where I lived.
Did you ever play with Wade Whaley, the Claremanist?
Oh, man. Yeah. Oh, I like to see Wade.
We couldn't find him in California. Fess and I tried to find him and already nobody knows where he is. I believe Wade.
I thought Wade had died.
He might be. He could well be.

Yeah, now we supplied in the district together with Piron. So, at the casino, and Wade Whaley, Black Pete, myself, and Piron, and four of us. Four, that's all. You never did. Piron ever used no until after the district went down. Did you ever know Black Pete's real name? That's all I ever know, little Black Pete. That's all I ever know. That's all I ever know. That's all this way he taught, little Black Pete. You remember him. No, I never knew him, but everybody.
You remember him?
That's all I know, Black Pete.
I was going to ask about Jimmy Noon too. Have you ever played with Jimmy down here? Sure.

Jimmy Noon was working with Manny Perez. He was nice, always was. Nice fella. A homely fella. They never catch him bumming after, you know. He and Manny Perez was playing at plays. Never catch him bumming. That's when my brother was playing there with them. But Brad Bebe, he was playing with them too, before they closed down. Jimmy Noon always was a nice fella. And Manny had a wonderful piano player, Frankie Haines. Oh yeah, I've heard of him. He was playing with them too. Manny, fella never did drink. Everything they played was strictly by music. Never did drink.
Jimbo must have been a pretty good reader too then, I guess. Who? Jimbo, Jimmy Noon. Jimmy Noon? Where's Brad? Yeah.
Where's Brad?
You know where he came from? Did you say he came from down the river? Yeah, still down the river. Down I'm from down there where Jimmy Noon. You see, you know.

Right down there. Round by Jell-O-Roll all of them come down here, come to God. Call him Jimbo. Yeah. Mhmm. I visited him when he was in Chicago playing up in the nest. Oh yes. There are little three pieces up there. I visited him. Wow.
Did you ever know Zoo Robertson on trombone? Zoo?

Zoo. I'm telling you I used to play with Zoo. Zoo was with the brass band. Mmhmm. Zoo was playing the brass band. Zoo was playing with the armored brass band. Zoo Robertson. Zoo Robertson. Noura Dutre. Rob Palmer. Vic Gasper. Field. And the old man Baptiste. Oh that was top musicians. You know. Top and Eddie Askin and all that fellas. Who? They never. They never. They never do that. Them. Yank. You know what you talk about Yanks? Yeah. Buddy Johnson. He was a popper. You see. A popper popper popper. You know. What about Dooson? What style did he have? Who? Frankie Dooson. Popper. He was a popper. Popper popper popper. You know. He was a popper. Yeah. Buddy Johnson. He was a popper. You see. A popper popper popper. You know. What about Dooson?
What style did he have? Who?
Frankie Dooson.
Popper.
He was a popper.
Popper.
Popper.
It's like Jim and him.

Yeah. I call all the best. Yeah. Them was. They used the trauma as a slice. And Laura Dutre. He was the only one. Every time you pull out orchestration. Where's my part? He didn't worry about no trauma part. Give me the shallow part. Ha. Ha. Ha. Ha. And Zu Raffling across his leg and make more stuff on the horn. The man can make on the saxophone.
How was Roy Palmer? What style did he have?

Palmer? Uh huh. Palmer was in between them. Roy Palmer. He was a good musician. Baratone and trombone. He played at the villa. One place, one spot all the time. Him and the old dude you see the old piano around you, play around you, all that you see. And he was playing there with Fess. Old Fess had charge of the band. I don't know if he told you about it. He mentioned it once.
Did you ever play with Fess at all? That's right. Have you played with Fess?

I played with Fess. My first lesson I took when I was learning how to read, I went to Fess and lived on Ellick Street in Algeria. He told me to get a little Tesson's Catechism. I said, boy you done improved mighty quick on that horn. Woo woo. I said, well begin from that catechism you start from. That's all. Like the people talk about Eddie Pearson. Steve Lewis was learning how to play trombone. And Steve Lewis didn't make you, bought a brand new horn. And Eddie Pearson come to my heart and say, that was, that was when I first married this guy, I said, I will learn how to play trombone like you. Eddie always was a man, you understand? He was in my class, you see Eddie. I was about seven, eight years old then but I mean we all come up together. See? I said, okay I'll learn you what I know. You know we're all together. I said, I learned Eddie was driving a truck right there for the cigar factory. I said, I'll learn you what I know. Like that. So he come back to my house over there in Algeria's. Started taking, well take lessons. He had a boss Steve Lewis home. I said, why don't you go to Vic? He taught me. So now I'm right over here with you. You can show me what you got but you know, I know the other fellas ain't going to do it. They won't take time out and ask them. I said, how about Fess? He said, Fess will show you. Fess didn't charge him too much money. He wants something for nothing. I said, I've been a young man, you know. So I said, okay. I said, first man, line eight is where the B flat was on the horn and everything. He took last one he bought, say about a year and eight months. Well, we had to go over the lake, you know. So we had to go over the lake every summer and I come back and be waiting. When I come in, he start telling what to do, the books and everything. And so next time he went to Fess. So Fess said, man, that boy sure doesn't improve on that horn. You sure? He said, you told him. I said, well. I told him all I know Fess. That's all I could do. He said, yeah, he doesn't improve. I can't do nothing with him. So Ada was gone. He told lots of people, many people that I taught him. It's like little Bob Aran right now. He learned him how to play. He learned him how to read drum music. George Williams. Nice. We learned him. Happy. We learned him. Had to learn Happy because we had the big band. They had Cecil Thornton, a great arranger from St. Louis. You don't know him. He had come down and he joined the Celestate band and he was the one that put Ricard to back. Trent Celestate band. He started arrangements there. He ceased the thorn. He was good on it. He was working on the cap. He got him a wife from now and he stayed down there and he started arranging for Papa Celestate. That's why he had put so much stuff on Ricard on the shoppers. I tell him that all the time. Even in fact, St. Louis, he's still in the mail service now. I can think so much about this life.
Yeah, there's so many people you know.

I used to go follow my brother. Not follow him, but I used to tell him to come at the economy hall and places to help him with his drum like that. I used to carry a drum across the third district ferry. He'd bring the drum backward and forward then. Get up there and I'd play. You know, listen, I didn't play a while. I had this cap on going on. See, hi him, hi him, hi Matthews, hi Billy, hi Billy.
Kept on. Did I ask you if you still have a drum set? Did you save your drums?
I said, it's a big picture right back there. I have a Zooty Singleton. It's on there right now. He said, oh pal, Bill, I'll never forget you of what you did for me. I give Zooty my set of drums.
Oh, Zooty got them.

To learn on. When I went away, my drum. I said, yeah, take them. I had to talk, I was teaching him. I said, now you take them. You get a break, they're yours. So Zooty started playing around here. When I was away, he said, right now, I said, right here. In his big picture, right there now. Old pal Bill, I'll never forget what you did for me. I have never seen Zooty since I left Chicago. But he had a wonderful set of drums at that time. But he think about what I did for him. I said, it seems Zooty. I can leave home now and go with friends I know. Friends I'm talking about. I was the first one to give Ray Allen his break. Why did they call him Biffley? Because he probably couldn't talk good, Biffley. He started a little. At that time. He couldn't talk good. He made a blues.
He made a record called Biffley Blues.

I never knew what that meant. That's how they called him over in Algiers. All them boys he raised. Allen and Sidney Dazby used to play with old man Allen brass band. Did you ever play in old man Allen's band? Sure. I got all this on the paper but I couldn't get to it before he was coming. That was my first out in the street. Old man Allen. I was playing right there with my brother. My brother Remus. He was playing the bass drum. I played the snare drum. Old man Joe Howe and all of us. Yeah. Papa Celestine was right there too.
He had the rehearsal.
Right in the Allen house. Mm-hmm. So that was the first one when I went on the street outside that little field band. Yeah. You doop, Yeah.
That's our dance. I wondered about Ramus, your oldest brother. Which brass band did he work with?

Allen was his famous band. That was the main one. Allen, the old man Henry Allen brass band. Mm-hmm. Was his favorite band. And he played bass drummers there. He was strictly the bass drum player in that band because...

Allen's brother was a snare drum player, George Allen. He lived over there, but he went back home and died in Morgan City. He got two old cities. Did he play in any of the other bands? Yeah, he played extra with the other bands. Like I tell you, he played extra with me. When I was, they tell me to get the Trummel House in Barnes, they tell me, I said, well they had to do this right across the street for me. He said, Bill, you play Trummel today, get your brother on a drum. I said, okay, we have a funeral like that, I said, I can't get off. I said, huh? I'll get a dream or something. They had three, four, five funerals a week like that. I said, Allison, sometimes he play with his orchestra, you know. I said, you play with the brass band, because I was waking every night out in Lake David, Piron Ambulance. He said, you play Trummel and use your brother on snare drum. He said, okay. I said, okay, we'll tell him.
Did he ever play any dance bands much? Remus?
My brother, Remus? Yes. Never had. Never did play. No more than at the fairground. Then they have two bands, had brass band at the fairground and, you know, orchestra and the side and stuff.
And you mentioned Bebe played with Lindsey and then he played with Manuel Perez. Was there any other bands that you remember?
Other bands too. He was one of the first, I mean one of the hit snare drum players in the Humboldt band, my brother's been big. Yeah.
Did he ever play with any of the other dance bands like Celestan or the Superior or any of
those? Yes.

Bay Bay. That was his band, the Superior band, orchestra. He played in that band. Oh, it's pitching in the paper. He used to play with all the old gasp and them, and I'm going to raise them, that's what I tell you. I used to help him carry the drums and play with them. Was that Imperial or Superior? Imperial. Imperial.

Imperial. Yeah, the Imperial and Superior. They see bands, them days they didn't go by a man's name. They didn't go by a man's name, they didn't go by a man's name, they didn't go by a man's name like you go by a certain person, they didn't go that way, they go taking the name. Now when me and Sammy Morgan was playing together, Sammy Morgan was playing with the Magnolia band. Yeah. You understand, the Magnolia band, Sammy Morgan was playing trumpet. But one had a band, Buddy Petit and John Robichaud, they didn't even by their band. But Buddy Petit had his own band like that, you know, his name. And from that they all started to sing like that. And Risley, he made up his band out of Jack Sheen. And they call it the, you know, Risley's band.
Yeah.

But before that, Babe, Babe Risley always was managing. Babe, Babe Risley had Peter Borkard, no, and P-Rone on violin. I think, I know P-Rone was on violin. T-O on clanging, Risley on trombone, Celeste on conant, I think it's George Foster on bass, Ernest Rapinoe on snare drum. And who was playing piano at that time? I think it was Freddie, no, Freddie wasn't playing. Freddie was playing by himself all the time.
The Freddie Washington?

Mm-hmm. He wasn't playing. He didn't play much out, you know. So they'd open up the, that's when things begin to, the Wolf begin to ride in the red lights, you know. Yeah. Begin to close them down in different places. And so they are, he used to play at the Tuxedo dance hall. So Risley taking that from that, and had the Tuxedo band. Yeah. You know what I'm saying? Risley take it from the head, see the Tuxedo band. That's why P-Rone, he pull out, and he made his P-Rone's band, see. So that's when it took Peter Borkard to lead there. Yes. Peter Borkard to lead there. I'm kind of thinking now. So that is, it still held Celestein anyway. Yeah. And he, this went on to tell you, lately they fell out about one dollar, a big business. Yeah.
Just one dollar.
One dollar. That's your guy. One dollar.
Did you ever know Freddie Kepard at all?
Oh sure. He knew him. Freddie Kepard, they're talking about jazz in New Orleans. Freddie Kepard. Big guy Louie, called Louie Nelson.
You know.

Eddie Garland. Eddie Vincent on Trauma from Al J. Yeah. That was the first Dixley band left here with me Sophie Tucker on the circus, in the Arthur Theater, the Arthur Circus. That was years ago. He wasn't born. No, no. I just heard some records or something. Well there wasn't records made like them, there was cup records there. Yeah. With them cups. I heard Sophie Tucker, and she was infamous.
How did Freddie Kepard play? What style was he?

I'm telling you, see, just like a- Was he more like Bowlin? Just like Bowlin and all that stuff. Just like Bowlin and all that stuff. But the thing about Freddie Kepard, he was more of a musician than Bowlin. You understand? He could play more late numbers. Them days you'd take five or six numbers and play them all night. But Freddie and them, they were musicians. You understand? They had music classes there. Musicians.
It was a yeah. I was a-
